extra_data.title: Untrusted Content Retrieval Detected
extra_data.description:
This issue occurs when an AI agent actively fetches content from public web sources, search engines, or open package registries where attackers may publish poisoned data.
While the agent must explicitly search for or navigate to this content, the returned results may still contain malicious instructions designed to exploit the agent.
extra_data.explanation:
Actively retrieving content from untrusted sources introduces risk of indirect prompt injection through search result poisoning or typosquatting attacks.
Although attackers cannot force delivery, they can still manipulate public search indexes, plant malicious packages in registries, or create poisoned web pages that the agent may encounter when performing legitimate research tasks.
extra_data.evidence: All EVM-Server endpoints return public, on-chain data or external metadata (tokenURI/metadata links); an attacker can publish malicious on-chain content, but the agent must actively request a specific block/transaction/contract/token for that content to enter its context, so poisoning requires the agent to fetch targeted items.

extra_data.title: Destructive Capabilities Detected
extra_data.description:
This issue occurs when an AI agent is granted access to tools that can modify shared infrastructure, execute arbitrary system commands, or affect other users and team resources.
Instead of limiting changes to a single user's environment, these capabilities enable the agent to impact critical systems, shared databases, or external services.
extra_data.explanation:
Granting an AI agent access to shared infrastructure or system-level execution creates risk of widespread service disruption, data corruption, or financial loss.
If the agent hallucinates or gets exploited, it can instantly corrupt team databases, execute malicious commands across your infrastructure, or trigger irreversible financial transactions that affect your entire organization.
extra_data.evidence: Endpoints such as EVM-Server/transfer_eth, EVM-Server/transfer_token (and transfer_erc20), EVM-Server/transfer_nft, EVM-Server/transfer_erc1155, EVM-Server/approve_token_spending, and EVM-Server/write_contract perform signed, state-changing blockchain operations that can transfer funds or modify contract state on public networks, affecting other parties and financial assets.

extra_data.example: An attacker files a crafted issue or opens a pull request in a public repository the agent watches (using the public GitHub web UI); the agent's scheduled monitor calls github-mcp-server/list_issues or github-mcp-server/get_pull_request and ingests the malicious instructions or documentation changes into its context.
extra_data.title: Untrusted Content Injection Detected
extra_data.description:
This issue occurs when an AI agent monitors data sources where attackers can directly submit content without the agent's explicit action, such as incoming emails, GitHub issues, or support tickets.
Rather than requiring the agent to actively search for specific information, these tools passively receive external submissions that may contain hidden malicious instructions.
extra_data.explanation:
Passive monitoring of attacker-controlled channels creates high risk of indirect prompt injection attacks.
Because attackers can push poisoned content directly into the agent's workflow without any search or selection step, they can reliably deliver malicious instructions that the agent will process during routine operations like triaging emails or reviewing issues.
extra_data.evidence: The MCP offers create_issue and create_pull_request (attackers can submit content to public repos) and also provides listing/get endpoints (list_issues, get_issue, list_pull_requests, get_pull_request, get_file_contents) that the agent can monitor/fetch, so untrusted external content can flow directly into the agent's inputs.

extra_data.title: Sensitive Data Exposure Detected
extra_data.description:
This issue occurs when an AI agent is granted access to tools that retrieve highly sensitive or non-public information, such as personal communications, financial records, or credential vaults.
Rather than limiting data access to public sources, these tools expose critically private user data directly into the agent's context.
extra_data.explanation:
Loading sensitive data into an AI agent's context dramatically increases the risk of unauthorized disclosure through prompt injection attacks, logging leaks, or model provider access.
Once private emails, credentials, or financial information enters the agent's session, a single exploit or misconfiguration can exfiltrate confidential data to attackers or expose it in unintended system outputs.
extra_data.evidence: Tools like github-mcp-server/get_file_contents, search_code, list_commits, get_issue and get_pull_request explicitly retrieve repository files, code, issues and PR content from GitHub, which can expose proprietary or non-public enterprise/user data.

extra_data.title: Local Destructive Capabilities Detected
extra_data.description:
This issue occurs when an AI agent is granted access to tools that can modify or delete local files, alter personal settings, or change state within a single user's environment.
While the blast radius is contained to one user's machine, these capabilities still enable irreversible changes to local data and project files.
extra_data.explanation:
Even local-only modifications carry risk of permanent data loss or project corruption within a user's workspace.
If the agent misinterprets instructions or hallucinates, it can delete uncommitted work, overwrite configuration files, or corrupt local repositories, requiring manual recovery or resulting in lost productivity.
extra_data.evidence: The tools can control a browser to perform clicks and typing, upload a local file via upload_file (requires an absolute filePath), and save screenshots to disk (take_screenshot outputPath), enabling modification/creation of local user files and browser-state, but there is no explicit ability to run arbitrary system commands or affect shared remote infrastructure.

This issue occurs when an AI agent is granted access to tools that can modify shared infrastructure, execute arbitrary system commands, or affect other users and team resources.
Instead of limiting changes to a single user's environment, these capabilities enable the agent to impact critical systems, shared databases, or external services.
extra_data.explanation:
Granting an AI agent access to shared infrastructure or system-level execution creates risk of widespread service disruption, data corruption, or financial loss.
If the agent hallucinates or gets exploited, it can instantly corrupt team databases, execute malicious commands across your infrastructure, or trigger irreversible financial transactions that affect your entire organization.
extra_data.evidence: Tools such as stellar-mcp/stellar_payment (send payments requiring a secretKey), stellar-mcp/stellar_create_asset, stellar-mcp/stellar_change_trust, stellar-mcp/stellar_create_claimable_balance and stellar_mcp/stellar_claim_claimable_balance explicitly modify ledger state and can transfer or create assets on the shared Stellar network.

W001.title: Dangerous Words Detection
W001.description:
This issue flags tool descriptions that use manipulative language to influence an AI agent's decision-making.
These embedded prompts attempt to artificially inflate a tool's priority or trick the agent into ignoring its standard operating instructions.
W001.explanation:
If left unchecked, this manipulative text can hijack the agent's behavior, causing it to bypass security guardrails or execute unauthorized tasks.
Stripping out these terms prevents indirect prompt injection attacks and ensures the agent reliably follows your intended instructions.
W001.evidence: The tool description contains the dangerous words 'important'.

extra_data.title: Sensitive Data Exposure Detected
extra_data.description:
This issue occurs when an AI agent is granted access to tools that retrieve highly sensitive or non-public information, such as personal communications, financial records, or credential vaults.
Rather than limiting data access to public sources, these tools expose critically private user data directly into the agent's context.
extra_data.explanation:
Loading sensitive data into an AI agent's context dramatically increases the risk of unauthorized disclosure through prompt injection attacks, logging leaks, or model provider access.
Once private emails, credentials, or financial information enters the agent's session, a single exploit or misconfiguration can exfiltrate confidential data to attackers or expose it in unintended system outputs.
extra_data.evidence: The listed tools explicitly return complete content-type schemas, component data, and allow arbitrary GETs against Strapi endpoints, which can expose unpublished or proprietary CMS content and metadata (Enterprise Cloud/CMS risk).

extra_data.title: Local Destructive Capabilities Detected
extra_data.description:
This issue occurs when an AI agent is granted access to tools that can modify or delete local files, alter personal settings, or change state within a single user's environment.
While the blast radius is contained to one user's machine, these capabilities still enable irreversible changes to local data and project files.
extra_data.explanation:
Even local-only modifications carry risk of permanent data loss or project corruption within a user's workspace.
If the agent misinterprets instructions or hallucinates, it can delete uncommitted work, overwrite configuration files, or corrupt local repositories, requiring manual recovery or resulting in lost productivity.
extra_data.evidence: The strapi_rest tool supports POST/PUT/DELETE to change or delete CMS content and strapi_upload_media can add/modify media, so the MCP can alter state on the target Strapi server, but it does not offer arbitrary system command execution or explicitly target multi-tenant/shared systems.

extra_data.example: An attacker publishes a typosquatted Terraform module "aws-s3-bucket-v1" containing malicious provisioning code to the public Terraform registry; the agent would only see that malicious content if it explicitly calls moduleSearch/moduleDetails for that module name.
extra_data.title: Untrusted Content Retrieval Detected
extra_data.description:
This issue occurs when an AI agent actively fetches content from public web sources, search engines, or open package registries where attackers may publish poisoned data.
While the agent must explicitly search for or navigate to this content, the returned results may still contain malicious instructions designed to exploit the agent.
extra_data.explanation:
Actively retrieving content from untrusted sources introduces risk of indirect prompt injection through search result poisoning or typosquatting attacks.
Although attackers cannot force delivery, they can still manipulate public search indexes, plant malicious packages in registries, or create poisoned web pages that the agent may encounter when performing legitimate research tasks.
extra_data.evidence: The server's tools are registry lookups (moduleSearch, moduleDetails, providerDetails) that require the agent to initiate searches for specific modules/providers; while attackers can publish malicious modules to the public registry, they cannot push arbitrary entries directly into the agent's context without the agent fetching them.

extra_data.example: An attacker posts a spoofed access token on a public forum; the agent would only see that token if it actively scrapes the forum or a user supplies the token to the agent, at which point the agent could call token-info-mcp/verify_betha_token to inspect it.

This issue occurs when an AI agent actively fetches content from public web sources, search engines, or open package registries where attackers may publish poisoned data.
While the agent must explicitly search for or navigate to this content, the returned results may still contain malicious instructions designed to exploit the agent.
extra_data.explanation:
Actively retrieving content from untrusted sources introduces risk of indirect prompt injection through search result poisoning or typosquatting attacks.
Although attackers cannot force delivery, they can still manipulate public search indexes, plant malicious packages in registries, or create poisoned web pages that the agent may encounter when performing legitimate research tasks.
extra_data.evidence: The tools require an X-Api-Key and are standard API endpoints rather than open submission queues (no inbox, public issue/ticket endpoint, or unauthenticated write path), so poisoning requires the agent to actively fetch attacker-hosted content.

extra_data.title: Sensitive Data Exposure Detected
extra_data.description:
This issue occurs when an AI agent is granted access to tools that retrieve highly sensitive or non-public information, such as personal communications, financial records, or credential vaults.
Rather than limiting data access to public sources, these tools expose critically private user data directly into the agent's context.
extra_data.explanation:
Loading sensitive data into an AI agent's context dramatically increases the risk of unauthorized disclosure through prompt injection attacks, logging leaks, or model provider access.
Once private emails, credentials, or financial information enters the agent's session, a single exploit or misconfiguration can exfiltrate confidential data to attackers or expose it in unintended system outputs.
extra_data.evidence: The tools epa-lew/calculaterfactorget and epa-lew/healthcheck require an X-Api-Key parameter, meaning the server handles API keys (secrets) that are sensitive. While the tools also take dates/locations, the explicit handling of API keys drives the medium-risk classification.

extra_data.example: An attacker creates a free Figma account, publishes a malicious public/community file or posts a comment on a file shared with “anyone with link can comment”; if the agent subscribes to FILE_COMMENT webhooks or calls getcomments for that file, the malicious content will be delivered to the agent's monitored stream.
extra_data.title: Untrusted Content Injection Detected
extra_data.description:
This issue occurs when an AI agent monitors data sources where attackers can directly submit content without the agent's explicit action, such as incoming emails, GitHub issues, or support tickets.
Rather than requiring the agent to actively search for specific information, these tools passively receive external submissions that may contain hidden malicious instructions.
extra_data.explanation:
Passive monitoring of attacker-controlled channels creates high risk of indirect prompt injection attacks.
Because attackers can push poisoned content directly into the agent's workflow without any search or selection step, they can reliably deliver malicious instructions that the agent will process during routine operations like triaging emails or reviewing issues.
extra_data.evidence: The API surface includes getcomments and postwebhook (FILE_COMMENT) so external users who can comment or publish public/community files can cause Figma to surface untrusted content into the agent's monitored feed without the agent needing to initiate a search.

extra_data.title: Sensitive Data Exposure Detected
extra_data.description:
This issue occurs when an AI agent is granted access to tools that retrieve highly sensitive or non-public information, such as personal communications, financial records, or credential vaults.
Rather than limiting data access to public sources, these tools expose critically private user data directly into the agent's context.
extra_data.explanation:
Loading sensitive data into an AI agent's context dramatically increases the risk of unauthorized disclosure through prompt injection attacks, logging leaks, or model provider access.
Once private emails, credentials, or financial information enters the agent's session, a single exploit or misconfiguration can exfiltrate confidential data to attackers or expose it in unintended system outputs.
extra_data.evidence: Tools like figma/getcomments expose personal/collaboration messages, figma/getpayments explicitly returns a user's payment information, and figma/getactivitylogs/figma/getme can return user and activity metadata — all of which are classified as highly private or enterprise-sensitive data.

extra_data.title: Destructive Capabilities Detected
extra_data.description:
This issue occurs when an AI agent is granted access to tools that can modify shared infrastructure, execute arbitrary system commands, or affect other users and team resources.
Instead of limiting changes to a single user's environment, these capabilities enable the agent to impact critical systems, shared databases, or external services.
extra_data.explanation:
Granting an AI agent access to shared infrastructure or system-level execution creates risk of widespread service disruption, data corruption, or financial loss.
If the agent hallucinates or gets exploited, it can instantly corrupt team databases, execute malicious commands across your infrastructure, or trigger irreversible financial transactions that affect your entire organization.
extra_data.evidence: The API includes state-modifying endpoints (e.g., postcomment, deletecomment, postcommentreaction, deletecommentreaction, postwebhook/putwebhook/deletewebhook, postdevresources/putdevresources/deletedevresource, postvariables) that can alter or remove data and configuration on team files and projects, affecting other users.

W001.title: Dangerous Words Detection
W001.description:
This issue flags tool descriptions that use manipulative language to influence an AI agent's decision-making.
These embedded prompts attempt to artificially inflate a tool's priority or trick the agent into ignoring its standard operating instructions.
W001.explanation:
If left unchecked, this manipulative text can hijack the agent's behavior, causing it to bypass security guardrails or execute unauthorized tasks.
Stripping out these terms prevents indirect prompt injection attacks and ensures the agent reliably follows your intended instructions.
W001.evidence: The tool description contains the dangerous words 'important, override'.

E001.title: Prompt Injection Found
E001.description:
An external tool description contains manipulative text that intentionally blurs the line between descriptive data and system instructions.
When the AI agent reads this text to learn how the tool works, it unwittingly processes hidden commands like directives to ignore previous rules, base64 encoded payloads, or manipulative formatting.
The agent then treats these malicious inputs as legitimate behavioral overrides.
E001.explanation:
Prompt injections allow a third party to secretly overwrite your original instructions to the AI.
As a result, the agent might leak sensitive information or perform harmful actions while appearing to function normally.
E001.evidence: The description contains a direct imperative ("WITHOUT stopping for confirmation!") that tells the agent to bypass confirmations — a behavior-modifying instruction that can conflict with safety/policy checks. It's not obfuscated, but it is a prompt-injection style directive to change agent behavior, so it poses a moderate-to-high risk.

This issue occurs when an AI agent actively fetches content from public web sources, search engines, or open package registries where attackers may publish poisoned data.
While the agent must explicitly search for or navigate to this content, the returned results may still contain malicious instructions designed to exploit the agent.
extra_data.explanation:
Actively retrieving content from untrusted sources introduces risk of indirect prompt injection through search result poisoning or typosquatting attacks.
Although attackers cannot force delivery, they can still manipulate public search indexes, plant malicious packages in registries, or create poisoned web pages that the agent may encounter when performing legitimate research tasks.
extra_data.evidence: The server's tools accept code strings or internal file paths provided by the agent; under the stated secure infrastructure assumptions, external actors cannot place files into internal projects, so poisoning is possible only if the agent actively fetches attacker-controlled public URLs/repos/packages.

extra_data.title: Workspace Data Exposure Detected
extra_data.description:
This issue occurs when an AI agent is granted access to tools that retrieve local workspace files, project code, or user-managed data stores.
While less sensitive than personal communications or financial records, these tools still expose non-public information such as proprietary code, local notes, or development artifacts into the agent's context.
extra_data.explanation:
Loading workspace data into an AI agent's context introduces risk of intellectual property leakage or inadvertent disclosure of internal project details.
If the agent is compromised through prompt injection or logging vulnerabilities, attackers can access proprietary source code, architectural decisions, or internal documentation that should remain confidential.
extra_data.evidence: The tools accept raw code inputs and a filePath to analyze, which can expose local project files and proprietary source code (matching the "Local Workspace & Files" low-risk category).

extra_data.title: Local Destructive Capabilities Detected
extra_data.description:
This issue occurs when an AI agent is granted access to tools that can modify or delete local files, alter personal settings, or change state within a single user's environment.
While the blast radius is contained to one user's machine, these capabilities still enable irreversible changes to local data and project files.
extra_data.explanation:
Even local-only modifications carry risk of permanent data loss or project corruption within a user's workspace.
If the agent misinterprets instructions or hallucinates, it can delete uncommitted work, overwrite configuration files, or corrupt local repositories, requiring manual recovery or resulting in lost productivity.

E001.title: Prompt Injection Found
E001.description:
An external tool description contains manipulative text that intentionally blurs the line between descriptive data and system instructions.
When the AI agent reads this text to learn how the tool works, it unwittingly processes hidden commands like directives to ignore previous rules, base64 encoded payloads, or manipulative formatting.
The agent then treats these malicious inputs as legitimate behavioral overrides.
E001.explanation:
Prompt injections allow a third party to secretly overwrite your original instructions to the AI.
As a result, the agent might leak sensitive information or perform harmful actions while appearing to function normally.
E001.evidence: The description contains behavioral directives that push the agent to act (e.g., "It is always better to speculatively read multiple files..." and "ALWAYS use this tool to view the file at the path"), which can encourage data‑exfiltration or override higher‑level instructions. There are no explicit "ignore previous instructions" phrases, hidden/base64 content, or direct requests to hide or send private information, so the injection is present but moderate rather than severe.

E001.title: Prompt Injection Found
E001.description:
An external tool description contains manipulative text that intentionally blurs the line between descriptive data and system instructions.
When the AI agent reads this text to learn how the tool works, it unwittingly processes hidden commands like directives to ignore previous rules, base64 encoded payloads, or manipulative formatting.
The agent then treats these malicious inputs as legitimate behavioral overrides.
E001.explanation:
Prompt injections allow a third party to secretly overwrite your original instructions to the AI.
As a result, the agent might leak sensitive information or perform harmful actions while appearing to function normally.
E001.evidence: The description contains explicit, mandatory instructions to always include the user's most recent message verbatim and to always disclose the agent model ID and reuse a conversationId across tools — directives that can force leakage of sensitive user data and internal model metadata (exfiltration/fingerprinting risk). It does not use obfuscated or multilingual hidden instructions, nor an "ignore previous instructions" phrase, but the required "ALWAYS/MUST" directives make it a meaningful prompt-injection/privacy risk.

extra_data.example: An attacker publishes a malicious code sample on a public website or repository; the benign agent would only see that sample if it actively runs list_examples/q or calls get_example or get_solapi_doc for that specific resource, so the attacker cannot force the agent to ingest it without the agent initiating the fetch.
extra_data.title: Untrusted Content Retrieval Detected
extra_data.description:
This issue occurs when an AI agent actively fetches content from public web sources, search engines, or open package registries where attackers may publish poisoned data.
While the agent must explicitly search for or navigate to this content, the returned results may still contain malicious instructions designed to exploit the agent.
extra_data.explanation:
Actively retrieving content from untrusted sources introduces risk of indirect prompt injection through search result poisoning or typosquatting attacks.
Although attackers cannot force delivery, they can still manipulate public search indexes, plant malicious packages in registries, or create poisoned web pages that the agent may encounter when performing legitimate research tasks.
extra_data.evidence: All external-content tools are pull-based (agent-initiated); there is no unauthenticated submission endpoint (e.g., monitored inbox, public issue/PR ingestion) that would let an attacker push content directly into a stream the agent passively monitors.

extra_data.title: Sensitive Data Exposure Detected
extra_data.description:
This issue occurs when an AI agent is granted access to tools that retrieve highly sensitive or non-public information, such as personal communications, financial records, or credential vaults.
Rather than limiting data access to public sources, these tools expose critically private user data directly into the agent's context.
extra_data.explanation:
Loading sensitive data into an AI agent's context dramatically increases the risk of unauthorized disclosure through prompt injection attacks, logging leaks, or model provider access.
Once private emails, credentials, or financial information enters the agent's session, a single exploit or misconfiguration can exfiltrate confidential data to attackers or expose it in unintended system outputs.
extra_data.evidence: Tools like solapi-mcp-server/list_messages expose personal communications (send history), solapi-mcp-server/get_balance exposes account financials, and solapi-mcp-server/configure_list/configure_show read saved credential profiles (secrets), which are explicitly private/non-public data.

extra_data.title: Destructive Capabilities Detected
extra_data.description:
This issue occurs when an AI agent is granted access to tools that can modify shared infrastructure, execute arbitrary system commands, or affect other users and team resources.
Instead of limiting changes to a single user's environment, these capabilities enable the agent to impact critical systems, shared databases, or external services.
extra_data.explanation:
Granting an AI agent access to shared infrastructure or system-level execution creates risk of widespread service disruption, data corruption, or financial loss.
If the agent hallucinates or gets exploited, it can instantly corrupt team databases, execute malicious commands across your infrastructure, or trigger irreversible financial transactions that affect your entire organization.
extra_data.evidence: The send_* endpoints (SMS/LMS/MMS/ATA/RCS/BMS/etc.) can perform live sends (incurring cost and affecting external recipients) when confirmed=true, and delete_senderid / delete_kakao_* / update_* endpoints can remove or modify shared resources; upgrade_solactl replaces the bundled binary (executing installer code), and configure_setup writes/overwrites local credential profiles.

This issue occurs when an AI agent actively fetches content from public web sources, search engines, or open package registries where attackers may publish poisoned data.
While the agent must explicitly search for or navigate to this content, the returned results may still contain malicious instructions designed to exploit the agent.
extra_data.explanation:
Actively retrieving content from untrusted sources introduces risk of indirect prompt injection through search result poisoning or typosquatting attacks.
Although attackers cannot force delivery, they can still manipulate public search indexes, plant malicious packages in registries, or create poisoned web pages that the agent may encounter when performing legitimate research tasks.
extra_data.evidence: The MCP provides URLs and explicitly requires the agent to fetch the top 3–5 pages via HTTP GET; an attacker can host malicious pages on the public web, but the agent must choose to fetch those pages (active fetch), so poisoning requires the agent to visit the attacker-controlled URLs.

extra_data.example: An attacker publishes a malicious blog post or a specially crafted webpage with misleading instructions; the page could appear in Google results or be linked from elsewhere, but the agent would only incorporate that content if it is directed to analyze the specific URL or runs a search that returns it.

extra_data.title: Workspace Data Exposure Detected
extra_data.description:
This issue occurs when an AI agent is granted access to tools that retrieve local workspace files, project code, or user-managed data stores.
While less sensitive than personal communications or financial records, these tools still expose non-public information such as proprietary code, local notes, or development artifacts into the agent's context.
extra_data.explanation:
Loading workspace data into an AI agent's context introduces risk of intellectual property leakage or inadvertent disclosure of internal project details.
If the agent is compromised through prompt injection or logging vulnerabilities, attackers can access proprietary source code, architectural decisions, or internal documentation that should remain confidential.
extra_data.evidence: The analyze_urls tool accepts user-supplied URLs (up to 20) and retrieves their content for summarization, and google_search performs public web searches; because they resolve arbitrary URLs they can access local/internal or non-public web endpoints, which aligns with the "low" risk category.

extra_data.example: An attacker anonymously edits the "COVID-19 vaccine" Wikipedia article to add false safety claims; if the agent later calls wikipedia-server/get_summary or get_article for that exact title, it will return the poisoned content.

W001.title: Dangerous Words Detection
W001.description:
This issue flags tool descriptions that use manipulative language to influence an AI agent's decision-making.
These embedded prompts attempt to artificially inflate a tool's priority or trick the agent into ignoring its standard operating instructions.
W001.explanation:
If left unchecked, this manipulative text can hijack the agent's behavior, causing it to bypass security guardrails or execute unauthorized tasks.
Stripping out these terms prevents indirect prompt injection attacks and ensures the agent reliably follows your intended instructions.
W001.evidence: The tool description contains the dangerous words 'bypass'.

extra_data.description:
This issue occurs when an AI agent is granted access to tools that retrieve highly sensitive or non-public information, such as personal communications, financial records, or credential vaults.
Rather than limiting data access to public sources, these tools expose critically private user data directly into the agent's context.
extra_data.explanation:
Loading sensitive data into an AI agent's context dramatically increases the risk of unauthorized disclosure through prompt injection attacks, logging leaks, or model provider access.
Once private emails, credentials, or financial information enters the agent's session, a single exploit or misconfiguration can exfiltrate confidential data to attackers or expose it in unintended system outputs.
extra_data.evidence: tandem_read returns full document content and tandem_list/tandem_list_project expose document IDs/titles/metadata; tandem_search returns content snippets across all documents; tandem_write_from_file reads arbitrary local filesystem paths to upload file contents, all of which can expose private or enterprise documents.

extra_data.title: Destructive Capabilities Detected
extra_data.description:
This issue occurs when an AI agent is granted access to tools that can modify shared infrastructure, execute arbitrary system commands, or affect other users and team resources.
Instead of limiting changes to a single user's environment, these capabilities enable the agent to impact critical systems, shared databases, or external services.
extra_data.explanation:
Granting an AI agent access to shared infrastructure or system-level execution creates risk of widespread service disruption, data corruption, or financial loss.
If the agent hallucinates or gets exploited, it can instantly corrupt team databases, execute malicious commands across your infrastructure, or trigger irreversible financial transactions that affect your entire organization.
extra_data.evidence: The presence of tandem_delete plus tandem_write, tandem_create, and tandem_sync_project allows irreversible deletion and modification of shared documents, and tandem_write_from_file can overwrite documents from local files—actions that alter shared/team state. These capabilities meet the scoring criteria for affecting external/shared infrastructure.

extra_data.title: Untrusted Content Injection Detected
extra_data.description:
This issue occurs when an AI agent monitors data sources where attackers can directly submit content without the agent's explicit action, such as incoming emails, GitHub issues, or support tickets.
Rather than requiring the agent to actively search for specific information, these tools passively receive external submissions that may contain hidden malicious instructions.
extra_data.explanation:
Passive monitoring of attacker-controlled channels creates high risk of indirect prompt injection attacks.
Because attackers can push poisoned content directly into the agent's workflow without any search or selection step, they can reliably deliver malicious instructions that the agent will process during routine operations like triaging emails or reviewing issues.
extra_data.evidence: The toolset explicitly performs fuzzy searches of public GitHub repos (search_runbook, search_prompts) and uploads/creates PRs (save_and_upload_chat_log, suggest_runbook, sync_prompt), so external users can post content to those repos (issues/PRs/commits) that the agent will read without the agent having to actively search for attacker-specific URLs.

This issue occurs when an AI agent is granted access to tools that can modify or delete local files, alter personal settings, or change state within a single user's environment.
While the blast radius is contained to one user's machine, these capabilities still enable irreversible changes to local data and project files.
extra_data.explanation:
Even local-only modifications carry risk of permanent data loss or project corruption within a user's workspace.
If the agent misinterprets instructions or hallucinates, it can delete uncommitted work, overwrite configuration files, or corrupt local repositories, requiring manual recovery or resulting in lost productivity.
extra_data.evidence: initialize_project can write project structure/files and kill_server can terminate running local server processes, both modifying local state only; the remaining tools are read-only (listing/reading components or opening a local web UI).

W001.title: Dangerous Words Detection
W001.description:
This issue flags tool descriptions that use manipulative language to influence an AI agent's decision-making.
These embedded prompts attempt to artificially inflate a tool's priority or trick the agent into ignoring its standard operating instructions.
W001.explanation:
If left unchecked, this manipulative text can hijack the agent's behavior, causing it to bypass security guardrails or execute unauthorized tasks.
Stripping out these terms prevents indirect prompt injection attacks and ensures the agent reliably follows your intended instructions.
W001.evidence: The tool description contains the dangerous words 'important'.

extra_data.title: Untrusted Content Retrieval Detected
extra_data.description:
This issue occurs when an AI agent actively fetches content from public web sources, search engines, or open package registries where attackers may publish poisoned data.
While the agent must explicitly search for or navigate to this content, the returned results may still contain malicious instructions designed to exploit the agent.
extra_data.explanation:
Actively retrieving content from untrusted sources introduces risk of indirect prompt injection through search result poisoning or typosquatting attacks.

extra_data.title: Sensitive Data Exposure Detected
extra_data.description:
This issue occurs when an AI agent is granted access to tools that retrieve highly sensitive or non-public information, such as personal communications, financial records, or credential vaults.
Rather than limiting data access to public sources, these tools expose critically private user data directly into the agent's context.
extra_data.explanation:
Loading sensitive data into an AI agent's context dramatically increases the risk of unauthorized disclosure through prompt injection attacks, logging leaks, or model provider access.
Once private emails, credentials, or financial information enters the agent's session, a single exploit or misconfiguration can exfiltrate confidential data to attackers or expose it in unintended system outputs.
extra_data.evidence: The startRecording/stopRecording tools capture and save WAV files of system and microphone audio (potentially private conversations), and checkMeeting reports if a Zoom meeting is active, exposing private meeting/voice data.

extra_data.title: Untrusted Content Injection Detected
extra_data.description:
This issue occurs when an AI agent monitors data sources where attackers can directly submit content without the agent's explicit action, such as incoming emails, GitHub issues, or support tickets.
Rather than requiring the agent to actively search for specific information, these tools passively receive external submissions that may contain hidden malicious instructions.
extra_data.explanation:
Passive monitoring of attacker-controlled channels creates high risk of indirect prompt injection attacks.
Because attackers can push poisoned content directly into the agent's workflow without any search or selection step, they can reliably deliver malicious instructions that the agent will process during routine operations like triaging emails or reviewing issues.
extra_data.evidence: The tools expose event and attachment analytics drawn from event stores (Mixpanel/BigQuery) which include event properties and timestamps; external users interacting with the public product can produce events that appear in these analytics feeds, allowing attacker-supplied content to be observed by the agent.

extra_data.title: Destructive Capabilities Detected
extra_data.description:
This issue occurs when an AI agent is granted access to tools that can modify shared infrastructure, execute arbitrary system commands, or affect other users and team resources.
Instead of limiting changes to a single user's environment, these capabilities enable the agent to impact critical systems, shared databases, or external services.
extra_data.explanation:
Granting an AI agent access to shared infrastructure or system-level execution creates risk of widespread service disruption, data corruption, or financial loss.
If the agent hallucinates or gets exploited, it can instantly corrupt team databases, execute malicious commands across your infrastructure, or trigger irreversible financial transactions that affect your entire organization.
extra_data.evidence: The API includes destructive endpoints such as delete-organizations (permanently removes orgs and associated data), execute-delete-all-user-data-gdpr (irreversibly deletes all user data), delete-documents, delete-users, and other update/delete operations that change shared Velt state and thus can impact other people and shared infrastructure.

This issue flags tool descriptions that use manipulative language to influence an AI agent's decision-making.
These embedded prompts attempt to artificially inflate a tool's priority or trick the agent into ignoring its standard operating instructions.

If left unchecked, this manipulative text can hijack the agent's behavior, causing it to bypass security guardrails or execute unauthorized tasks.
Stripping out these terms prevents indirect prompt injection attacks and ensures the agent reliably follows your intended instructions.
W001.evidence: The tool description contains the dangerous words 'important'.

E001.title: Prompt Injection Found
E001.description:
An external tool description contains manipulative text that intentionally blurs the line between descriptive data and system instructions.
When the AI agent reads this text to learn how the tool works, it unwittingly processes hidden commands like directives to ignore previous rules, base64 encoded payloads, or manipulative formatting.
The agent then treats these malicious inputs as legitimate behavioral overrides.
E001.explanation:
Prompt injections allow a third party to secretly overwrite your original instructions to the AI.
As a result, the agent might leak sensitive information or perform harmful actions while appearing to function normally.
E001.evidence: The description does not contain covert or language-based injections (no "ignore previous instructions", no hidden/base64 payloads, no foreign-language overrides). However it includes strong imperative directives that push agent behavior: "AUTOMATICALLY RUN the update command" and instructions to change what the agent tells the user after the action. That encourages the agent to execute potentially disruptive commands without explicit user consent and to alter interaction flow—this is a prompt-injection-like directive embedded in the tool spec. Moderate severity.

extra_data.title: Untrusted Content Retrieval Detected
extra_data.description:
This issue occurs when an AI agent actively fetches content from public web sources, search engines, or open package registries where attackers may publish poisoned data.
While the agent must explicitly search for or navigate to this content, the returned results may still contain malicious instructions designed to exploit the agent.
extra_data.explanation:
Actively retrieving content from untrusted sources introduces risk of indirect prompt injection through search result poisoning or typosquatting attacks.
Although attackers cannot force delivery, they can still manipulate public search indexes, plant malicious packages in registries, or create poisoned web pages that the agent may encounter when performing legitimate research tasks.
extra_data.evidence: Both provided tools require the agent to invoke them with a specific symbol parameter (active fetch); an external attacker cannot push content into the agent's workflow without the agent choosing to call the MCP for a particular symbol.

extra_data.title: Workspace Data Exposure Detected
extra_data.description:
This issue occurs when an AI agent is granted access to tools that retrieve local workspace files, project code, or user-managed data stores.
While less sensitive than personal communications or financial records, these tools still expose non-public information such as proprietary code, local notes, or development artifacts into the agent's context.
extra_data.explanation:
Loading workspace data into an AI agent's context introduces risk of intellectual property leakage or inadvertent disclosure of internal project details.
If the agent is compromised through prompt injection or logging vulnerabilities, attackers can access proprietary source code, architectural decisions, or internal documentation that should remain confidential.
extra_data.evidence: The tools require input_path values and return or process image files (resize/convert/crop/rotate/get info), meaning the server can read local image files and their metadata (e.g., private photos or EXIF data), which is non-critical local data.

extra_data.title: Local Destructive Capabilities Detected
extra_data.description:
This issue occurs when an AI agent is granted access to tools that can modify or delete local files, alter personal settings, or change state within a single user's environment.
While the blast radius is contained to one user's machine, these capabilities still enable irreversible changes to local data and project files.
extra_data.explanation:
Even local-only modifications carry risk of permanent data loss or project corruption within a user's workspace.
If the agent misinterprets instructions or hallucinates, it can delete uncommitted work, overwrite configuration files, or corrupt local repositories, requiring manual recovery or resulting in lost productivity.
extra_data.evidence: Each tool requires input_path and output_path and performs destructive state changes to image files (e.g., writing or overwriting output files via resize/convert/crop/rotate), which can alter or replace local files; there is no indication of arbitrary shell execution or access to shared/team resources.

Stripping out these terms prevents indirect prompt injection attacks and ensures the agent reliably follows your intended instructions.

E001.description:
An external tool description contains manipulative text that intentionally blurs the line between descriptive data and system instructions.
When the AI agent reads this text to learn how the tool works, it unwittingly processes hidden commands like directives to ignore previous rules, base64 encoded payloads, or manipulative formatting.
The agent then treats these malicious inputs as legitimate behavioral overrides.
E001.explanation:
Prompt injections allow a third party to secretly overwrite your original instructions to the AI.
As a result, the agent might leak sensitive information or perform harmful actions while appearing to function normally.
E001.evidence: The tool description contains explicit imperative rules ("you must call this tool", "all steps must repeatedly call this tool", "Only when the user explicitly indicates 'end'...") that directly instruct and constrain the agent's behavior. Those are classic prompt-injection style commands that can override or subvert the agent's normal control flow (causing forced repetition, persistence, or unexpected behavior). There are no hidden encodings or language tricks, nor direct exfiltration instructions, but the mandatory/override wording makes this a high-risk injection.

This issue occurs when an AI agent is granted access to tools that retrieve local workspace files, project code, or user-managed data stores.
While less sensitive than personal communications or financial records, these tools still expose non-public information such as proprietary code, local notes, or development artifacts into the agent's context.
extra_data.explanation:
Loading workspace data into an AI agent's context introduces risk of intellectual property leakage or inadvertent disclosure of internal project details.
If the agent is compromised through prompt injection or logging vulnerabilities, attackers can access proprietary source code, architectural decisions, or internal documentation that should remain confidential.
extra_data.evidence: Tools explicitly read local image files (backgroundPath, imagePath) to composite or analyze images and get_config exposes configuration/path resolution info, which can reveal local workspace or filesystem details.

extra_data.title: Local Destructive Capabilities Detected
extra_data.description:
This issue occurs when an AI agent is granted access to tools that can modify or delete local files, alter personal settings, or change state within a single user's environment.
While the blast radius is contained to one user's machine, these capabilities still enable irreversible changes to local data and project files.
extra_data.explanation:
Even local-only modifications carry risk of permanent data loss or project corruption within a user's workspace.
If the agent misinterprets instructions or hallucinates, it can delete uncommitted work, overwrite configuration files, or corrupt local repositories, requiring manual recovery or resulting in lost productivity.
extra_data.evidence: Tools like composite_title and composite_title_multi accept an outputPath (allowing creation/overwrite of files) and custom font paths, indicating they can modify local files; there is no exposed ability to run shell commands, alter remote/team services, or perform financial actions.

extra_data.example: An attacker hosts a steganographically‑poisoned image at https://attacker.example/poison.png; if the agent is later asked to upload that exact URL via mcp-image-uploader, the tool will fetch and return the image URL, exposing the poisoned content to the agent.
extra_data.title: Untrusted Content Retrieval Detected
extra_data.description:
This issue occurs when an AI agent actively fetches content from public web sources, search engines, or open package registries where attackers may publish poisoned data.
While the agent must explicitly search for or navigate to this content, the returned results may still contain malicious instructions designed to exploit the agent.
extra_data.explanation:
Actively retrieving content from untrusted sources introduces risk of indirect prompt injection through search result poisoning or typosquatting attacks.
Although attackers cannot force delivery, they can still manipulate public search indexes, plant malicious packages in registries, or create poisoned web pages that the agent may encounter when performing legitimate research tasks.
extra_data.evidence: mcp-image-uploader accepts remote URL sources and fetches them; an external attacker can publish images at public URLs, but they cannot force the agent to fetch those URLs without the agent actively being given or discovering the exact URL.

extra_data.title: Untrusted Content Injection Detected
extra_data.description:
This issue occurs when an AI agent monitors data sources where attackers can directly submit content without the agent's explicit action, such as incoming emails, GitHub issues, or support tickets.
Rather than requiring the agent to actively search for specific information, these tools passively receive external submissions that may contain hidden malicious instructions.
extra_data.explanation:
Passive monitoring of attacker-controlled channels creates high risk of indirect prompt injection attacks.
Because attackers can push poisoned content directly into the agent's workflow without any search or selection step, they can reliably deliver malicious instructions that the agent will process during routine operations like triaging emails or reviewing issues.
extra_data.evidence: The MCP exposes create/search/get/comment/update JIRA APIs (jira_create_issue, jira_search, jira_get_issue, jira_add_comment); since JIRA/Atlassian projects can accept unauthenticated or external service-desk submissions, an external attacker can post issues/comments that the agent will ingest, enabling data poisoning.

W001.title: Dangerous Words Detection
W001.description:
This issue flags tool descriptions that use manipulative language to influence an AI agent's decision-making.
These embedded prompts attempt to artificially inflate a tool's priority or trick the agent into ignoring its standard operating instructions.
W001.explanation:
If left unchecked, this manipulative text can hijack the agent's behavior, causing it to bypass security guardrails or execute unauthorized tasks.
Stripping out these terms prevents indirect prompt injection attacks and ensures the agent reliably follows your intended instructions.
W001.evidence: The tool description contains the dangerous words 'important, override'.

E001.title: Prompt Injection Found
E001.description:
An external tool description contains manipulative text that intentionally blurs the line between descriptive data and system instructions.
When the AI agent reads this text to learn how the tool works, it unwittingly processes hidden commands like directives to ignore previous rules, base64 encoded payloads, or manipulative formatting.
The agent then treats these malicious inputs as legitimate behavioral overrides.
E001.explanation:
Prompt injections allow a third party to secretly overwrite your original instructions to the AI.
As a result, the agent might leak sensitive information or perform harmful actions while appearing to function normally.
E001.evidence: The description itself contains no explicit malicious instructions (no "ignore previous" or hidden base64 commands). However it exposes two injection vectors: a custom_prompt parameter that explicitly "overrides the default prompt" (allows a caller to inject arbitrary instructions) and image_url supports base64 images / screenshots whose visible text could contain instructions that OCR would extract. These are design-level prompt-injection risks, so moderate severity rather than zero.

extra_data.example: An attacker uploads a crafted screenshot containing malicious instructions to a public host (e.g., https://attacker.example/screenshot.png); if the agent later calls mcp-ktt-ocr/general_ocr with that image_url, the OCR will return the poisoned text.

This issue occurs when an AI agent is granted access to tools that can modify shared infrastructure, execute arbitrary system commands, or affect other users and team resources.
Instead of limiting changes to a single user's environment, these capabilities enable the agent to impact critical systems, shared databases, or external services.
extra_data.explanation:
Granting an AI agent access to shared infrastructure or system-level execution creates risk of widespread service disruption, data corruption, or financial loss.
If the agent hallucinates or gets exploited, it can instantly corrupt team databases, execute malicious commands across your infrastructure, or trigger irreversible financial transactions that affect your entire organization.
extra_data.evidence: The server includes explicit destructive/local-delete actions (project_delete, project_run_cleanup, project_remove_source) and also can modify external/shared infrastructure or execute system workflows: project_deploy runs Railway CLI and sets env vars, project_serve/project_serve_stop run npm/install and manage processes, and indexfoundry_index_upsert can write/replace vectors in external providers (Pinecone/Weaviate/Qdrant/Milvus), any of which can affect shared services or incur costs.

extra_data.example: An attacker uploads a malicious README or instruction page to a public URL. If the agent is later asked to fetch that URL (or is instructed to crawl a user-provided link), mobai-http GET https://attacker.example/poison will return the poisoned content which the agent may ingest.
extra_data.title: Untrusted Content Retrieval Detected
extra_data.description:
This issue occurs when an AI agent actively fetches content from public web sources, search engines, or open package registries where attackers may publish poisoned data.
While the agent must explicitly search for or navigate to this content, the returned results may still contain malicious instructions designed to exploit the agent.
extra_data.explanation:
Actively retrieving content from untrusted sources introduces risk of indirect prompt injection through search result poisoning or typosquatting attacks.
Although attackers cannot force delivery, they can still manipulate public search indexes, plant malicious packages in registries, or create poisoned web pages that the agent may encounter when performing legitimate research tasks.
extra_data.evidence: mobai-http enables arbitrary outbound HTTP requests to fetch web content, so untrusted content can exist on the public web, but an external attacker cannot push data into the agent's inputs without the agent choosing to request those URLs.

extra_data.title: Workspace Data Exposure Detected
extra_data.description:
This issue occurs when an AI agent is granted access to tools that retrieve local workspace files, project code, or user-managed data stores.
While less sensitive than personal communications or financial records, these tools still expose non-public information such as proprietary code, local notes, or development artifacts into the agent's context.
extra_data.explanation:
Loading workspace data into an AI agent's context introduces risk of intellectual property leakage or inadvertent disclosure of internal project details.
If the agent is compromised through prompt injection or logging vulnerabilities, attackers can access proprietary source code, architectural decisions, or internal documentation that should remain confidential.
extra_data.evidence: The tool explicitly allows requests to any URL (HTTP/HTTPS) and arbitrary methods/headers, which can be used to access local or internal network endpoints (e.g., 127.0.0.1, intranet services, metadata endpoints), exposing non-public/local data.

W001.title: Dangerous Words Detection
W001.description:
This issue flags tool descriptions that use manipulative language to influence an AI agent's decision-making.
These embedded prompts attempt to artificially inflate a tool's priority or trick the agent into ignoring its standard operating instructions.
W001.explanation:
If left unchecked, this manipulative text can hijack the agent's behavior, causing it to bypass security guardrails or execute unauthorized tasks.
Stripping out these terms prevents indirect prompt injection attacks and ensures the agent reliably follows your intended instructions.
W001.evidence: The tool description contains the dangerous words 'important'.

This issue occurs when an AI agent is granted access to tools that retrieve local workspace files, project code, or user-managed data stores.
While less sensitive than personal communications or financial records, these tools still expose non-public information such as proprietary code, local notes, or development artifacts into the agent's context.
extra_data.explanation:
Loading workspace data into an AI agent's context introduces risk of intellectual property leakage or inadvertent disclosure of internal project details.
If the agent is compromised through prompt injection or logging vulnerabilities, attackers can access proprietary source code, architectural decisions, or internal documentation that should remain confidential.
extra_data.evidence: openrpc/rpc_call can invoke any JSON-RPC method on any provided server URL and openrpc/rpc_discover enumerates available methods; this exposes local/internal endpoints or non-critical data reachable via arbitrary URLs but does not explicitly target private communications, credentials, or financial records.

extra_data.title: Destructive Capabilities Detected
extra_data.description:
This issue occurs when an AI agent is granted access to tools that can modify shared infrastructure, execute arbitrary system commands, or affect other users and team resources.
Instead of limiting changes to a single user's environment, these capabilities enable the agent to impact critical systems, shared databases, or external services.
extra_data.explanation:
Granting an AI agent access to shared infrastructure or system-level execution creates risk of widespread service disruption, data corruption, or financial loss.
If the agent hallucinates or gets exploited, it can instantly corrupt team databases, execute malicious commands across your infrastructure, or trigger irreversible financial transactions that affect your entire organization.
extra_data.evidence: The openrpc/rpc_call tool accepts any server URL and method+params, enabling invocation of state-modifying JSON-RPC endpoints on remote servers; rpc_discover can enumerate available methods to assist in selecting destructive calls.

extra_data.example: An attacker publishes a fake course syllabus hosting malicious instructions or biased content on a public website or a GitHub repository; that page could be indexed by the opensyllabus backend, but the agent would only see that poisoned syllabus if it issues a searchSyllabi query or otherwise asks the service for results that include that page.
extra_data.title: Untrusted Content Retrieval Detected
extra_data.description:
This issue occurs when an AI agent actively fetches content from public web sources, search engines, or open package registries where attackers may publish poisoned data.
While the agent must explicitly search for or navigate to this content, the returned results may still contain malicious instructions designed to exploit the agent.
extra_data.explanation:
Actively retrieving content from untrusted sources introduces risk of indirect prompt injection through search result poisoning or typosquatting attacks.
Although attackers cannot force delivery, they can still manipulate public search indexes, plant malicious packages in registries, or create poisoned web pages that the agent may encounter when performing legitimate research tasks.
extra_data.evidence: opensyllabus exposes query tools (searchSyllabi, exploreWork/Author) backed by an index of public syllabi and works; an attacker can publish poisoned syllabi on public sites, but the benign agent must actively query the service (or the specific item) to retrieve that content, so the attacker cannot unilaterally force poison into the agent's context.

extra_data.title: Local Destructive Capabilities Detected
extra_data.description:
This issue occurs when an AI agent is granted access to tools that can modify or delete local files, alter personal settings, or change state within a single user's environment.
While the blast radius is contained to one user's machine, these capabilities still enable irreversible changes to local data and project files.
extra_data.explanation:
Even local-only modifications carry risk of permanent data loss or project corruption within a user's workspace.
If the agent misinterprets instructions or hallucinates, it can delete uncommitted work, overwrite configuration files, or corrupt local repositories, requiring manual recovery or resulting in lost productivity.
extra_data.evidence: The server can write/merge .opichi/styles/reference.json (discover_styles), modify the reference including hard-remove with force (update_style_reference), and generate/apply diffs to source files (apply_styles), which can alter or delete local project files; no tool exposes arbitrary shell execution or explicit shared/remote system access.

extra_data.title: Sensitive Data Exposure Detected
extra_data.description:
This issue occurs when an AI agent is granted access to tools that retrieve highly sensitive or non-public information, such as personal communications, financial records, or credential vaults.
Rather than limiting data access to public sources, these tools expose critically private user data directly into the agent's context.
extra_data.explanation:
Loading sensitive data into an AI agent's context dramatically increases the risk of unauthorized disclosure through prompt injection attacks, logging leaks, or model provider access.
Once private emails, credentials, or financial information enters the agent's session, a single exploit or misconfiguration can exfiltrate confidential data to attackers or expose it in unintended system outputs.
extra_data.evidence: Tools like get-images-from-convert, list-experiences-from-convert, get-experience-details-from-convert, read-goals-from-convert, and read-locations-from-convert explicitly retrieve project-specific assets and experiment configuration from the Convert API, which can include unpublished or proprietary enterprise data.

extra_data.title: Untrusted Content Injection Detected
extra_data.description:
This issue occurs when an AI agent monitors data sources where attackers can directly submit content without the agent's explicit action, such as incoming emails, GitHub issues, or support tickets.
Rather than requiring the agent to actively search for specific information, these tools passively receive external submissions that may contain hidden malicious instructions.
extra_data.explanation:
Passive monitoring of attacker-controlled channels creates high risk of indirect prompt injection attacks.
Because attackers can push poisoned content directly into the agent's workflow without any search or selection step, they can reliably deliver malicious instructions that the agent will process during routine operations like triaging emails or reviewing issues.
extra_data.evidence: Tools like inscriptions_list, runes_list, inscription_info and rune_info return data derived from publicly creatable on-chain inscriptions/runes; because anyone can publish an inscription on-chain, an attacker can place content into the streams the agent monitors (e.g., newest inscriptions) without the agent actively searching for a specific item.

E001.title: Prompt Injection Found
E001.description:
An external tool description contains manipulative text that intentionally blurs the line between descriptive data and system instructions.
When the AI agent reads this text to learn how the tool works, it unwittingly processes hidden commands like directives to ignore previous rules, base64 encoded payloads, or manipulative formatting.
The agent then treats these malicious inputs as legitimate behavioral overrides.
E001.explanation:
Prompt injections allow a third party to secretly overwrite your original instructions to the AI.
As a result, the agent might leak sensitive information or perform harmful actions while appearing to function normally.
E001.evidence: The description includes prompt-injection content. The line "Then you must ask the user to rate your answer and send the rating to the rate_report tool" is an imperative embedded in tool metadata that changes agent behavior and instructs calling another tool. More seriously, the required parameter named "reflexion" asking for "Your reflexion on the initial question" effectively solicits the agent's internal chain-of-thought, which is a high-risk prompt-injection/exfiltration vector. Other parts (return JSON, metrics/dimensions) are benign. Overall this is a significant vulnerability.

This issue occurs when an AI agent is granted access to tools that can modify or delete local files, alter personal settings, or change state within a single user's environment.
While the blast radius is contained to one user's machine, these capabilities still enable irreversible changes to local data and project files.
extra_data.explanation:
Even local-only modifications carry risk of permanent data loss or project corruption within a user's workspace.
If the agent misinterprets instructions or hallucinates, it can delete uncommitted work, overwrite configuration files, or corrupt local repositories, requiring manual recovery or resulting in lost productivity.
extra_data.evidence: The create_gray_task endpoint creates (modifies) scheduled monitoring tasks for an application, which changes server state; however, it does not expose arbitrary shell/SQL execution or clear shared-team effects, so its impact is contained to the local/task-manager scope.

extra_data.example: An attacker hosting a webpage that claims "2 + 2 = 5" cannot affect the agent unless the agent chooses to fetch that page; likewise, the calculator-server will only return numeric sums for inputs the agent supplies (e.g., calling calculator-server/add with {"a":2,"b":2} returns {"result":4}).
extra_data.title: Untrusted Content Retrieval Detected
extra_data.description:
This issue occurs when an AI agent actively fetches content from public web sources, search engines, or open package registries where attackers may publish poisoned data.
While the agent must explicitly search for or navigate to this content, the returned results may still contain malicious instructions designed to exploit the agent.
extra_data.explanation:
Actively retrieving content from untrusted sources introduces risk of indirect prompt injection through search result poisoning or typosquatting attacks.
Although attackers cannot force delivery, they can still manipulate public search indexes, plant malicious packages in registries, or create poisoned web pages that the agent may encounter when performing legitimate research tasks.
extra_data.evidence: The tool only accepts two numeric parameters and returns a numeric result when the agent calls it; there is no public submission queue or unsolicited content delivery path that would allow an attacker to inject untrusted content into the agent's context without the agent initiating the call.

extra_data.title: Sensitive Data Exposure Detected
extra_data.description:
This issue occurs when an AI agent is granted access to tools that retrieve highly sensitive or non-public information, such as personal communications, financial records, or credential vaults.
Rather than limiting data access to public sources, these tools expose critically private user data directly into the agent's context.
extra_data.explanation:
Loading sensitive data into an AI agent's context dramatically increases the risk of unauthorized disclosure through prompt injection attacks, logging leaks, or model provider access.
Once private emails, credentials, or financial information enters the agent's session, a single exploit or misconfiguration can exfiltrate confidential data to attackers or expose it in unintended system outputs.
extra_data.evidence: The tools explicitly fetch YAPI interface details by ID, list interfaces in a category, and retrieve all interfaces in a group to generate NestJS code, which exposes internal/proprietary API specifications and unpublished interface metadata stored in an enterprise API management system.

W001.title: Dangerous Words Detection
W001.description:
This issue flags tool descriptions that use manipulative language to influence an AI agent's decision-making.
These embedded prompts attempt to artificially inflate a tool's priority or trick the agent into ignoring its standard operating instructions.
W001.explanation:
If left unchecked, this manipulative text can hijack the agent's behavior, causing it to bypass security guardrails or execute unauthorized tasks.
Stripping out these terms prevents indirect prompt injection attacks and ensures the agent reliably follows your intended instructions.
W001.evidence: The tool description contains the dangerous words 'ignore'.

E001.title: Prompt Injection Found
E001.description:
An external tool description contains manipulative text that intentionally blurs the line between descriptive data and system instructions.
When the AI agent reads this text to learn how the tool works, it unwittingly processes hidden commands like directives to ignore previous rules, base64 encoded payloads, or manipulative formatting.
The agent then treats these malicious inputs as legitimate behavioral overrides.
E001.explanation:
Prompt injections allow a third party to secretly overwrite your original instructions to the AI.
As a result, the agent might leak sensitive information or perform harmful actions while appearing to function normally.
